title: Day of Parting, You Were Made Long
intro: Al-Suli and al-Tibrizi name Nuh ibn Amr al-Saksaki of Kinda as the man Abu Tammam praises. The poet makes us wait for him. A lover hears the call to depart as his own death sentence, reasons with himself about contentment, then takes us across the desert on a remarkably light-footed camel. The man waiting at the end offers one kind of closeness the opening had seemed to rule out, a friendship one would never regret.

translation: Day of parting, you were made long.
You have left me neither fortitude nor sense.
1.sharh: He addresses the day as a creature built to last. The length it takes from his life is measured in two distinct losses, endurance and the ability to think.

translation: If death’s scout lost his way, he would want
only parting to guide him to living souls.
2.sharh: A scout goes ahead to find a road. Separation knows exactly where death can find a soul, because it has already come so close to taking one.

translation: They called, “Time to go.” I had no doubt
it was my own soul setting out from this world.
3.sharh: The caravan's announcement reaches him as news about himself. We have to wait through the line break to learn who he thinks is departing.

translation: Patience is the finer thing, yet bewilderment
in love has the better claim to beauty.
4.sharh: The two halves keep the same word for beauty but revise the standard. In a lover, looking distractedly this way and that may be the more faithful response.

translation: Do you think I can find a way to consolation?
Death would sooner find its way to me.
5.sharh: The road changes direction mid-verse. He may never reach consolation, but death has no difficulty reaching him.

translation: Easier to turn a bolting, headstrong horse
than turn back a tear that has found its course.
6.sharh: A horse running away with its rider seems the greater force. Once a tear finds its channel, the comparison gives the smaller thing the greater momentum.

translation: The rain stars remembered you as I remember one of you.
They wept over you morning and evening.
7.sharh: His words go out to the whole departing company, his thought to one person in it. The seasons of rain appear to keep the same hours of mourning that he does.

translation: My life for the moon at Muhajjar,
kept safe from all but given over to separation.
8.sharh: The moon is the beloved. Guarding her from other people offers no protection against distance, which has free access to her.

translation: I looked hard at separation and found it
a sword drawn against me, with love beside it.
9.sharh: He can picture the harm only by giving separation a blade. Love stands alongside it, since his attachment makes distance capable of wounding him.

translation: Do not hold me to account for time. It does not
follow my orders, and I cannot stand surety for it.
10.sharh: Time might be a servant receiving orders, or a debtor for whom he gives a guarantee. Neither relationship is within a lover’s power.

translation: Whoever advances on the days and musters against them
anything but contentment will keep coming off defeated.
11.sharh: Time is an enemy against which one might draw troops up. The only force that survives the meeting is the capacity to live with what one has.

translation: Whoever pastures his resolve and his ambitions
in the meadow of wishes will always go lean.
12.sharh: Wishes offer ideal grazing to the eye. What they fail to put on the bones is substance, whether for a herd or for a person's purposes.

translation: If contentment’s rule and judgement held
among mankind, little would no longer be little.
13.sharh: The repeated “little” first measures an amount and then judges its sufficiency. Contentment can change the second verdict without changing the amount.

translation: Do not fret over your livelihood. It comes
though you have sent no messenger to fetch it.
14.sharh: Provision finds its own way to its recipient. The imagined errand takes the worry of waiting and gives it a practical job it never actually performed.

translation: What a marvel you are, crossing such a waste
without so much as startling the skittish ostrich.
15.sharh: He has turned to the camel he rides. Some commentators make the ostrich unafraid because it knows such a familiar traveller, others because she passes before it can take fright.

translation: Daughter of the open country, when she strides with you
she leaves no desert longing unassuaged in your breast.
16.sharh: The open country is her parent. What feels like a thirst in her rider’s chest can be satisfied by travelling through the desert on her back.

translation: Look at her. You cannot see her for the spring
that outstrips the eye, headlong at a swinging trot.
17.sharh: The command to look runs straight into the impossibility of seeing. The camel is already beyond the place to which the eye has just been directed.

translation: Had Ubayd ever given her an errand,
he would have forgotten Shadqam and Jadil.
18.sharh: The comparison calls in a judge who knew camels intimately. One journey on her would displace even two famous stud lines from his memory.

translation: In the man of Saksak, of Mati', ambitions found delight
and sent back time’s gaze exhausted.
19.sharh: The clan name Mati' and the verb for taking delight nearly chime. The eyes that gave up the chase in the preceding camel passage now belong to time itself.

translation: Never call Nuh ibn Amr
to meet a crisis unless it is immense.
20.sharh: The apparent restriction on asking for help is a compliment. A difficulty must first qualify as large enough to merit this man's attention.

translation: Alert when difficulties come visiting,
he meets them smiling, a man open-handed and noble.
21.sharh: The troubles themselves become visitors and take a good look at their host. His smile is the first thing they have to contend with.

translation: He keeps twisting them firm, till one might say
God never made a single, untwisted thread.
22.sharh: The praise depends on two stages in making cord. Nuh's hands have been so busy twisting loose strands together that nobody can remember ever seeing one on its own.

translation: Steady on his feet, he sees a tribe as one man.
A company sees him and takes him for a company.
23.sharh: The shift from seeing to being seen reverses the arithmetic. Many look like one to him, while to them a single figure looks like many.

translation: How many great battles you have fought for noble deeds,
leaving all you owned dead on the field.
24.sharh: The casualty is identified only in the second half. Winning a battle in generosity means having little of one's own property left standing.

translation: You sent a raid through the land of stinginess
that levelled the rough ground of misfortune.
25.sharh: Stinginess has territory that can be overrun. The advantage of that raid falls to the people whose formerly difficult road now lies level.

translation: You counted the most you gave away a trifle,
the least you were thanked for a great deal.
26.sharh: Gift and thanks are assessed by the same giver. His habit of undervaluing one and overvaluing the other lets a recipient escape the burden of an equal return.

translation: A man leaves no glory unclaimed when he makes generosity
his agent over his wealth for all who ask.
27.sharh: Generosity has power of attorney over the estate. A petitioner can deal with an agent whose very nature is to grant the request.

translation: Did Amr not spread generosity among the people
until we positively longed to find a miser?
28.sharh: The father's example has supposedly caught on so thoroughly that a miser would be a welcome curiosity. The joke makes public influence a family inheritance.

translation: Grip Nuh’s rope tight in both hands.
You will find it joined to generosity itself.
29.sharh: A rope can be clutched for safety, and a bond of protection can be called a rope. Either way the far end is attached to generosity.

translation: With him for your close friend you will never say,
“If only I had never taken him for a friend.”
30.sharh: The close echoes the regret over a chosen companion in Qur'an 25.28. Praise takes the form of words this friend will never give anyone cause to utter.

1.2.4.head: جَلَد
1.2.4.meaning: Fortitude or staying power under strain.

1.2.6.head: مَعقول
1.2.6.meaning: The power of reason or judgement.

2.1.3.head: مُرتاد
2.1.3.meaning: A scout who searches ahead for a route or a stopping place.

2.1.4.head: مَنِيَّة
2.1.4.meaning: Appointed death, here imagined sending out its own scout.

3.1.2.head: الرَّحيل
3.1.2.meaning: Departure, here the call for the company to move off.

4.1.5.head: تَلَدُّد
4.1.5.meaning: Distracted looking about, as when a person is shaken or at a loss.

5.1.5.meaning: Consolation after a loss. The final syllable of the usual Arabic form is shortened.

5.2.2.head: حِمام
5.2.2.meaning: Death, distinguished by its vowel from the word for doves.

6.1.2.head: جَموح
6.1.2.meaning: A mount that bolts and is too strong for its rider.

6.2.6.head: مَسيل
6.2.6.meaning: A watercourse, here the channel a tear finds.

7.1.2.head: نَوء
7.1.2.meaning: The settings and risings of stars used to reckon seasons of rain.

7.2.4.head: أَصيل
7.2.4.meaning: Late afternoon, as daylight draws to its close.

8.1.1.head: بِنَفسي
8.1.1.meaning: “With my own life.” An offer to give oneself as ransom for the beloved.

8.1.4.head: مُحَجَّر
8.1.4.meaning: Muhajjar, the place where the moonlike beloved is staying.

8.2.3.head: نَوى
8.2.3.meaning: Separation or the distance between people who love one another.

10.2.1.head: تَبَع
10.2.1.meaning: A follower subject to another's command.

10.2.5.head: كَفيل
10.2.5.meaning: A guarantor who answers for someone else.

11.1.2.meaning: To advance against an opposing battle line.

11.1.5.meaning: Marshalled or drew up as for battle. The usual final hamza is eased.

11.2.5.head: مَفلول
11.2.5.meaning: Routed or blunted, as when a blade loses its edge.

12.1.3.meaning: Pasture, both the grazing ground and what feeds an animal there.

13.1.4.head: قُنوع
13.1.4.meaning: Contentment. The noun can elsewhere mean asking, but the preceding verse supplies the sense here.

14.1.3.head: كَمِدَ
14.1.3.meaning: To fret or brood over something.

15.1.2.head: لِلَّهِ دَرُّكِ
15.1.2.meaning: An exclamation of admiration directed here at the she-camel.

15.2.3-4.head: اِبن البَيضَة
15.2.3-4.meaning: “Son of the egg.” The male ostrich.

15.2.5.head: إِجفيل
15.2.5.meaning: Readily startled, always on the point of taking flight.

16.1.4.head: وَخَدَ
16.1.4.meaning: To travel at a camel's easy, rapid stride.

16.2.6.head: غَليل
16.2.6.meaning: Burning thirst or an unsatisfied longing.

17.2.1.head: شَأى
17.2.1.meaning: To outstrip, here to get beyond the reach of sight.

18.1.4.head: عُبَيد
18.1.4.meaning: Ubayd, identified by al-Suli as the poet al-Ra'i al-Numayri. Another explanation makes him a camel doctor.

18.2.3-4.head: شَدقَم وَجَديل
18.2.3-4.meaning: Shadqam and Jadil, famous stallion camels from which prized lines traced their descent.

19.1.1-2.head: السَّكسَكِيّ الماتِعِيّ
19.1.1-2.meaning: Al-Saksaki al-Mati'i, names connecting Nuh to his kin in Kinda.

19.2.5.head: كَليل
19.2.5.meaning: Weary or dulled, here of a gaze exhausted by trying to keep up.

20.1.3-5.head: نوح بن عَمرو
20.1.3-5.meaning: Nuh ibn Amr, the Kinda patron praised in the poem. His father is named again near the end.

20.2.1.head: خَطب
20.2.1.meaning: A grave affair or public emergency.

21.1.5.head: عَرا
21.1.5.meaning: Visited or descended on someone, as troubles do here.

21.2.3.head: بُهلول
21.2.3.meaning: A genial, generous lord, a term of praise here.

22.1.3.head: أَبرَمَ
22.1.3.meaning: To settle things firmly, literally to twist loose strands into cord.

22.2.5.head: سَحيل
22.2.5.meaning: A single strand that has yet to be twined with another.

23.1.1-2.head: ثَبت المَقام
23.1.1-2.meaning: “Firm of footing.” One who holds steady when others might falter.

23.2.3.head: قَبيل
23.2.3.meaning: A company of people, who need not all share a common ancestor.

24.1.2.head: وَقعَة
24.1.2.meaning: A pitched encounter, transferred to the field of giving.

25.2.2.head: حَزن
25.2.2.meaning: Rough stretches of ground, opposed to the plains.

26.1.4.head: حَبا
26.1.4.meaning: To bestow freely as a mark of favour.

26.1.6.head: لُهى
26.1.6.meaning: Large gifts or grants of money.

27.2.3.head: مُعتَفٍ
27.2.3.meaning: Someone who calls on a person in hope of a gift.

27.2.4.head: وَكيل
27.2.4.meaning: An agent authorised to administer someone’s property.

28.1.2.head: عَمرو
28.1.2.meaning: Amr, Nuh's father, whom the poet credits with spreading his example.

29.1.5.head: مُعصِم
29.1.5.meaning: Holding fast to something for protection or support.

30.1.5.head: خِلّ
30.1.5.meaning: An intimate friend. The two halves use related words for this closeness.
